objectives: Segment taught l CVC words into phonemes.
Map each phoneme to the correct grapheme.
Spell l CVC words from spoken dictation.
Self-correct vowel and consonant spelling errors.
concepts: CVC spelling requires ordered phoneme segmentation.
Short-vowel selection changes the written word.
Self-correction starts by isolating the incorrect sound.

definitions.definition: The smallest unit of sound in a spoken word.
A letter or letter group representing a speech sound.
Separate a spoken word into its individual phonemes.

commonMistakes: Replacing l with a different consonant.
Writing letter names instead of graphemes.

basic: Spell taught l CVC words from dictation.
conceptual: Identify the phoneme represented by each written grapheme.
application: Repair CVC spelling errors by isolating the incorrect phoneme.
higherOrderThinking: Explain how changing one middle vowel changes the written CVC word.
mixedReview: Mix l CVC spelling with previously taught consonants and short vowels.

formulaOrFactBank: CVC spelling = phoneme sequence mapped to graphemes in order.
mistakeBasedRevision: If spelling is wrong, say the word slowly and identify the mismatched sound.
weakTopicRevision: Practise the weakest short-vowel pattern with fresh l CVC words.

activities.name: Sound boxes
steps: Say a taught l CVC word.
Push one counter for each phoneme.
Write one grapheme for each sound.

activities.name: Spell and repair
steps: Compare each sound with the spelling.

outcomes: Learner segments taught l CVC words accurately.
Learner maps phonemes to graphemes in order.
Learner spells taught l CVC words and self-corrects common errors.

questions.question: Which letters spell /l/ at the beginning of “lip”?
What letter should come after l in “lip”?
What is the final letter in “log”?
A learner hears /l/ /ɪ/ /p/. What should they do first to spell the word?
options: Map each sound to a letter in order.
Choose a word from a picture.

questions.question: A learner writes “lap” for the spoken word “lip.” Which sound needs checking?
A learner writes “rog” when asked to spell “log.” Which sound should be corrected?
Why is it useful to say each phoneme before writing?
options: It helps map each sound to the correct grapheme.
It removes the need to hear vowels.

questions.question: A learner spells “lug” correctly but cannot spell “leg.” What is the best next practice?
options: Contrast the middle vowel sounds and spell both words from dictation.

questions.question: After spelling several taught l CVC words accurately, what should follow?
options: Controlled l word-family reading and sentence spelling
